title: The Deccan Sultanates
description: An illustrated map of the Bahmani Sultanate and the five kingdoms that grew out of it, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar and Berar, from the revolt at Daulatabad in 1347 to Talikota and the Mughal conquest of Golconda in 1687.
note: Based on the Persian histories of Firishta and Tabataba, Portuguese accounts of Talikota and the buildings the sultans left. Several founding dates, the date of Talikota and the details of famous deaths differ between sources. The map is stylised and not to scale.

steps.title: Revolt at Daulatabad
steps.text: The Yadavas of Devagiri had ruled from this fort until Delhi annexed it, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq renamed it Daulatabad. His demands for money and harsh punishments drove the Deccan’s centurions (amiran-i sada), the officers who ran its districts, to revolt. In 1347 they took the fort and crowned one of their leaders, Hasan, as Alauddin Bahman Shah.
steps.today: Daulatabad Fort, near Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar), Maharashtra.

steps.title: A capital at Gulbarga
steps.text: Bahman Shah ruled from Gulbarga, which he renamed Ahsanabad. His son Muhammad Shah I fought Vijayanagara for the Raichur doab, between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, in a war of two centuries. The Great Mosque in Gulbarga fort, finished in 1367, is roofed entirely with domes. The Chishti saint Gesu Daraz settled in the city and died there in 1422.
steps.today: Kalaburagi, Karnataka: the fort mosque and the shrine (dargah) of Gesu Daraz.

steps.title: The move to Bidar
steps.text: Ahmad Shah I moved the capital to Bidar in about 1427 and built a new city there with a fort and palaces. His tomb at Ashtur, painted inside in gold and colour, became a shrine, because he was revered as a saint (wali). Bidriware, dark metal inlaid with silver, is named after the city.
steps.today: Bidar Fort and the Bahmani tombs at Ashtur, Karnataka.

steps.title: Mahmud Gawan’s college
steps.text: Mahmud Gawan, a merchant from Persia, became chief minister and won the Konkan coast, Goa included. In 1472 he built a college (madrasa) at Bidar, three storeys high and faced with coloured tiles. The court was split between Deccanis and newcomers from abroad (Afaqis). His enemies forged a letter, and in 1481 the sultan had him executed.
steps.today: The madrasa of Mahmud Gawan, Bidar: half ruined, with one tiled minaret standing.

steps.title: Five kingdoms
steps.text: After Gawan’s death the governors stopped obeying Bidar. Yusuf Adil Khan made himself independent at Bijapur, Ahmad Nizam al-Mulk at Ahmadnagar and Fathullah Imad al-Mulk in Berar, all about 1490, and Sultan Quli Qutb al-Mulk later did the same at Golconda. At Bidar the Barid family ruled in the sultan’s name, and the last Bahmani fled in about 1527.
steps.today: The Barid Shahi tombs, Bidar, Karnataka.

steps.title: Diamonds of Golconda
steps.text: Sultan Quli turned the mud fort of Golconda, near today’s Hyderabad, into the stronghold of the Qutb Shahi dynasty. Diamonds dug in the Krishna valley, around Kollur, were sold through the city, and ‘Golconda’ came to mean a source of great wealth. The Koh-i-Noor is often said to come from these mines, though its origin is not recorded.

steps.title: An alliance sealed by marriage
steps.text: The sultans fought each other as often as Vijayanagara, and its regent Aliya Rama Raya played them against one another; around 1560 his armies plundered Ahmadnagar. Alarmed, the sultans made peace among themselves. Husain Nizam Shah of Ahmadnagar married his daughter Chand Bibi to Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur, and four of the five joined against Rama Raya.

steps.title: The battle of Talikota
steps.text: The armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar met Vijayanagara’s near the Krishna river, at the place also called Rakkasa-Tangadi; Berar stayed away. Rama Raya, an old man by every account, was captured and beheaded, and his army broke. The victors sacked the city of Vijayanagara for months. The Vijayanagara Empire never recovered, but the alliance soon fell apart.
steps.today: Talikota, Vijayapura district, Karnataka; the battlefield is thought to lie to its south, by the Krishna.

steps.title: Ibrahim II, teacher of the world
steps.text: Ibrahim Adil Shah II became sultan of Bijapur as a boy in 1580. A musician and painter, he wrote the Kitab-i Nauras, songs in Dakhni that praise Saraswati and Ganesha alongside the Prophet and Sufi saints, and was called Jagadguru, ‘teacher of the world’. His tomb, the Ibrahim Rauza, is among the Deccan’s finest.

steps.title: Hyderabad and the Charminar
steps.text: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah outgrew Golconda and founded Hyderabad beside the Musi river; its centrepiece, the Charminar, ‘four minarets’, was finished in 1591. He wrote poems in Dakhni, an early form of Urdu, gathered into one of its first collections. A story that he named the city after a dancer, Bhagmati, is often told and disputed.

steps.title: Chand Bibi defends Ahmadnagar
steps.text: Akbar’s son Murad besieged Ahmadnagar in 1595. Chand Bibi, back from Bijapur, led its defence, and her men repaired a breach overnight; in 1596 the Mughals withdrew in return for the province of Berar. They came back in 1600. She died while negotiating, killed by her own soldiers in some accounts, and the city fell soon after.
steps.today: Ahmadnagar Fort; the hilltop tomb outside the city called Chand Bibi’s Palace belongs to a noble, Salabat Khan.

steps.title: Malik Ambar
steps.text: Malik Ambar, born in Ethiopia and sold as a slave, rose to command the Nizam Shahi army and crowned a new sultan himself. With Maratha horsemen he raided Mughal supply lines and avoided pitched battles. He founded Khadki, later renamed Aurangabad, and reorganised land revenue. Shahaji Bhosale, Shivaji’s father, served under him. The Mughals ended the kingdom in 1636.
steps.today: Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar), Maharashtra; Malik Ambar’s tomb is at Khuldabad.

steps.title: The Gol Gumbaz
steps.text: Muhammad Adil Shah, who died in 1656, lies under the Gol Gumbaz, ‘round dome’, one of the world’s largest domes, about 44 metres across inside. A whisper in its gallery can be heard on the far side. Bijapur now held lands south to Bangalore, but faced the Mughals in the north and a new rebel in the west, Shivaji.

steps.title: Aurangzeb takes Bijapur
steps.text: Aurangzeb came south to finish the Deccan wars himself. His army besieged Bijapur for some fifteen months, while famine and disease spread in the city and in his own camp. In September 1686 the young Sikandar Adil Shah surrendered and was taken away a prisoner. The Adil Shahi dynasty ended after nearly two centuries, and Bijapur began to empty.
steps.today: Vijayapura, Karnataka: the city walls and the Malik-e-Maidan, a great Adil Shahi gun on a bastion.

steps.title: The fall of Golconda
steps.text: Golconda’s sultan Abul Hasan, called Tana Shah, ruled through the Brahmin ministers Madanna and Akkanna, killed in a palace plot in 1686. The fort held out for eight months in 1687 until, by most accounts, an officer opened a gate. Abul Hasan was sent prisoner to Daulatabad, where the Bahmani story had begun, and died there in 1699.
steps.today: Golconda Fort and the Qutb Shahi tombs, Hyderabad.

steps.title: The Deccani inheritance
steps.text: The sultanates left more than ruins. Dakhni, the language of their poets, helped shape Urdu, and Deccani painting mixed Persian, Indian and European styles. In 1724 the Mughal governor Asaf Jah, Nizam al-Mulk, made himself ruler of the Deccan, and his heirs, the Nizams, ruled from Hyderabad until 1948. The Qutb Shahi tombs have been restored in recent years.
steps.today: The Qutb Shahi Heritage Park, Hyderabad, restored with the Aga Khan Trust for Culture from 2013.

items.name: Mahmud Gawan
items.text: Born in Gilan, by the Caspian Sea, Mahmud Gawan came to the Deccan as a trader and rose to be the Bahmanis’ chief minister. He reformed their provinces, won the Konkan coast and built the great college at Bidar. He wrote letters in fine Persian prose. His execution is often seen as the start of the kingdom’s break-up.

items.name: Chand Bibi
items.text: Daughter of Husain Nizam Shah of Ahmadnagar, Chand Bibi married Ali Adil Shah I of Bijapur and, after his death in 1580, acted as regent for his young nephew Ibrahim II. Back in Ahmadnagar, she led its defence against the Mughals in 1595. Painted on horseback in later pictures, she is remembered across the Deccan as a heroine.

items.name: Ibrahim Adil Shah II
items.text: Ibrahim II ruled Bijapur from 1580 until his death in 1627. He played the tambura, gathered musicians and painters at court and founded a new city of music, Nauraspur, outside Bijapur. His songs in the Kitab-i Nauras invoke Hindu gods and Muslim saints together. Under him Bijapur painting reached its height, and the kingdom expanded south.

items.name: Malik Ambar
items.text: Born in Ethiopia, Malik Ambar was sold as a slave in Baghdad and came to the Deccan, serving Chingiz Khan, the Ahmadnagar minister. Freed, he built an army of his own, held off Mughal armies for a quarter of a century and ran the Nizam Shahi kingdom as regent. Jahangir’s painters showed him as a defeated enemy.
